passage: After-school club note, Wednesday. Preeti came in furious. Her mother had taken her tablet at bedtime the night before, after two warnings, and Preeti said it was cheating because she was in the middle of a level. She slammed her pencil case shut. Later she said quietly, "I miss it." I told her that losing something fun hurts, and she admitted she had once hidden the tablet under her blanket. I asked what might work better than hiding it. She thought and said, "If we knew the time in advance, it wouldn't be a surprise." I suggested she ask her mother for a fixed schedule. On Friday she told me they had agreed one, and she looked lighter. — Mr Vijay, club supervisor

qa.q: Who took Preeti's tablet, and when?
qa.a: Her mother took it at bedtime the night before.

qa.q: What is Preeti really upset about underneath her fury, and what hints at it?
qa.a: She was upset at losing something fun; her quiet "I miss it" shows the hurt under the anger.

qa.q: Why is agreeing a fixed schedule a better choice for Preeti than hiding the tablet?
qa.a: With a known time there is no surprise to fight about and no need to sneak, and her mother can trust her more. 🙂

qa.q: How might Preeti's mother have seen that bedtime moment?
qa.a: As the end of a limit she had already warned about twice, when it was time to stop for the night.

grounding: A child furious at a parent taking her tablet admits she misses it and negotiates a fixed schedule.

passage: In the school waiting area before the parent-teacher meeting, Gopika's mother looked at her for a moment. "You look tired, Gopika. I've seen the light under your door late at night." Gopika's first thought was to snap back that it was her tablet and her business. But her mother's eyebrows were pulled together in a worried way, not an angry one. Then Mr Arnab called them in, and mentioned that Gopika had yawned through the first lesson twice that week. Gopika stared at her shoes. "Maybe... we could pick a time when the screen goes off?" she said. Her mother let out a breath and nodded. "Let's write it down together."

qa.q: Where did Gopika's mother say she looked tired?
qa.a: In the school waiting area before the parent-teacher meeting.

qa.q: Why did Gopika's snappy first thought fade?
qa.a: She saw that her mother's pulled-together eyebrows looked worried, not angry, so she understood the comment came from care.

qa.q: What small step did Gopika take that shows she can look after herself?
qa.a: She suggested picking a time when the screen goes off, and agreed to write the limit down together with her mother.

qa.q: What is it like for Gopika's mother when Gopika suggests a limit herself?
qa.a: She feels relief, shown by the breath she let out, because Gopika is listening and joining in rather than being told.

grounding: A child hears her mother's worry about tiredness from screen use and sets a limit together with her.

passage: The power had gone out again, and the afternoon in the village stretched flat and hot. Nitin grabbed his father's phone and scrolled, thumb flicking, not really watching anything. His neighbour Hafsa leaned over the wall with a chalk stub. "You look like a sleepy buffalo," she said. Nitin groaned, "I'm bored." "Good," said Hafsa, "that's when I get ideas." She drew a wobbly hopscotch on the courtyard floor. Nitin put the phone on the step, huffing. He added a crooked snail shell at the end, then a ladder, then a river to jump. By the time the light turned golden, the whole courtyard was a game and his ears were pink from laughing.

qa.q: What did Hafsa draw on the courtyard floor?
qa.a: She drew a wobbly hopscotch.

qa.q: What was Nitin feeling when he scrolled without really watching?
qa.a: Bored and restless; his flicking thumb and groan of "I'm bored" show he was just filling the time.

qa.q: What could Nitin try next time he is bored and reaches for the phone?
qa.a: He could draw, play outside or make up a game like the courtyard one, and see what ideas come.

qa.q: How does Hafsa see boredom?
qa.a: As the moment ideas start, which is why she says "Good" when Nitin says he is bored.

grounding: A bored child reaches for the phone, then finds a new game outdoors, illustrating boredom as a start for ideas.

passage: Dinner was in twenty minutes, and the cricket highlights were on. "Give it!" Farhan grabbed the remote off the arm of the sofa just as Naveen snatched it back. "It's my turn, you had the cartoons!" "No, you did!" They were both standing now, voices rising over the hum of the ceiling fan. Farhan felt his face go hot; he wanted the match, and he wanted to win the argument even more. Then their mother's voice came from the kitchen: "Should I decide, or will you two?" Farhan gulped, took the kitchen timer from the shelf, and set it. "Ten minutes each. You first, since I grabbed." Naveen blinked, then sat down.

qa.q: How long before dinner were the boys fighting over the remote?
qa.a: Dinner was in twenty minutes.

qa.q: What did Farhan want most while grabbing the remote?
qa.a: He wanted the match, and even more he wanted to win the argument, as his hot face shows.

qa.q: Which choice worked for the boys, and why?
qa.a: Using the kitchen timer and taking turns worked, because it was fair and stopped the shouting and grabbing.

qa.q: How might Naveen have felt when Farhan offered him the first turn?
qa.a: Surprised and probably a bit relieved, since he blinked and then sat down instead of arguing.

grounding: A child fights over the TV remote with his brother and switches to a timer for fair turns, under time pressure before dinner.

passage: You look sad that your friends are all online tonight, beta. Let me tell you about when I was eleven. I'm Anjali, your aunt. My friends, Joseph and the others, had started playing one online game every evening, and if I didn't join I felt lonely, like a chair nobody sat in. So I joined, for hours. Afterwards my head felt heavy and I was grumpy with everyone at home. I noticed that. So one Sunday I said, "Joseph, come play tag outside, just for an hour." He grumbled, but he came, and two others followed. We were sweaty and loud, and I felt lighter. We still played online sometimes, but not every evening.

qa.q: Who did Anjali ask to come and play tag outside?
qa.a: She asked Joseph to come and play tag outside.

qa.q: How did Anjali feel when she was not part of the online game?
qa.a: Lonely, like a chair nobody sat in.

qa.q: What did Anjali try instead of joining every evening?
qa.a: She noticed how she felt after long screen time and invited her friends to play outside.

qa.q: How might Joseph have seen Anjali's invitation to play tag?
qa.a: He grumbled at first, so he may have been reluctant, but he came, which suggests he was willing to be asked.

grounding: A child feels lonely when friends prefer online play, notices how long screen time leaves her feeling, and invites them outside.

passage: Counsellor's note. Farhan came to see me after class with red ears. He said quietly, "I watched a video I knew I shouldn't. It was meant for older people. I feel really embarrassed, and I thought you'd tell my father and I'd be in trouble." I thanked him for telling me and said that being curious is normal. I explained in simple words that some videos are for adults, not children, and answered the two questions he asked. I asked whether he'd like to tell his father with me beside him. He said yes. Afterwards his father listened, thanked him for being honest, and did not punish him. Farhan's shoulders dropped. — Mr Naveen, school counsellor

qa.q: What colour were Farhan's ears when he came to the counsellor?
qa.a: They were red.

qa.q: What was Farhan afraid of when he came to see the counsellor?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and thought he would be in trouble, since he assumed the counsellor would tell his father and he would be punished.

qa.q: How did Mr Naveen help Farhan feel safe again?
qa.a: He thanked Farhan for telling him, said curiosity is normal, answered his questions simply, and stayed beside him when he told his father.

qa.q: How might Farhan's father have felt hearing this?
qa.a: Probably concerned, but glad his son was honest, since he thanked Farhan and did not punish him.

grounding: A child ashamed of watching something unsuitable tells a trusted adult and is helped without being punished.

passage: Saturday: At lunch Madhav's grandfather Shankar pushed his rice around the plate. "You children never talk to me now. Only the phone." Madhav felt a hot flush of guilt and stared at his screen, glued to the corner. Sunday: In the evening Madhav put his phone in the drawer in the hall. "Dada, will you tell me a story?" Shankar's eyebrows shot up. He told about walking to school through mustard fields in bare feet. Madhav asked how far and whether there were snakes. The following Saturday: Shankar was waiting on the veranda with two cups of milk. "Story time?" he asked. Madhav grinned and ran to leave the phone inside.

qa.q: What did Shankar say the children did instead of talking to him?
qa.a: He said they only had the phone.

qa.q: What was Madhav feeling when his grandfather said the children never talk to him?
qa.a: Guilt; he felt a hot flush and stared at his screen.

qa.q: What did Madhav do that gave both of them something they needed?
qa.a: He put the phone away in the drawer and asked his grandfather for a story, which gave Shankar company and Madhav a good talk.

qa.q: What might Shankar have felt when Madhav asked for a story?
qa.a: Surprise and probably gladness, since his eyebrows shot up and the next Saturday he was waiting with milk.

grounding: A child feels guilty when his grandfather says phones keep the children from talking, then sets the phone aside for story time across days.

passage: "Suraj, beta, you haven't eaten anything." "I can't, Wasim bhai." Suraj's voice cracked. "Sheru's bowl is still by the door." "I know." "It hurts here." He pressed a fist to his chest. "Like there's a hole." "That's how it is when someone you love is gone. You can cry, Suraj. I cried too, in the bathroom." "You did?" "Yes. Sheru slept on my feet for years." Suraj sniffed. "Can I keep his collar?" "Of course. We could find a box for it, and his ball, and the photo from the beach." "And a drawing?" "A drawing too." Suraj wiped his nose on his sleeve. "Can we do it now?"

qa.q: Where was Sheru's bowl?
qa.a: It was still by the door.

qa.q: What does Suraj mean when he says there is a hole in his chest?
qa.a: He means his grief over losing Sheru feels like a real empty ache inside, which is why he cannot eat.

qa.q: What healthy ways of saying goodbye does the passage show?
qa.a: Crying, talking about the loss, and making a small memory box with the collar, the ball, a photo and a drawing. 🤍

qa.q: How does Wasim relate to Suraj's grief?
qa.a: He also loved Sheru, who slept on his feet for years, and cried in the bathroom too, so he shares the loss instead of just comforting.

grounding: A child grieves the death of his dog, cries and talks with his brother, and starts a memory box.

passage: Note from Ms Bhavna, class teacher. Minakshi came in very quiet on Monday and drew on the back of her notebook without speaking. At break I sat beside her and she said her cat had died on Sunday. "I cried at the kitchen table, and Papa hugged me. He said it's okay to cry. He didn't tell me to stop." Her voice was small but steady. "I felt less alone," she said. She said she had cried again that night, but not as much. I asked if she would like to tell the class about her cat, and she chose to draw a picture instead and put it on the board.

qa.q: Where did Minakshi cry on Sunday?
qa.a: She cried at the kitchen table.

qa.q: How did Minakshi feel after her father hugged her?
qa.a: She felt less alone, and it helped that he did not tell her to stop crying.

qa.q: How could a teacher support Minakshi at school?
qa.a: By sitting beside her, listening, and giving her a choice about how to share her cat, as Ms Bhavna did when Minakshi drew a picture. 🤍

qa.q: What might Minakshi's father have wanted when he hugged her and said it's okay to cry?
qa.a: To let her know that being sad is normal and that she did not have to carry it alone.

grounding: A child grieving her cat is comforted by her father's hug and permission to cry, noticed by her teacher.

passage: At recess in the Madrid schoolyard, Tomas sat on the bench with his sandwich untouched. His dog Luna had died on Saturday. Mateo dropped down beside him. "You're still sad? It's only a dog. Just get a new one." Tomas felt his throat tighten. Luna had waited at the door every afternoon; she was family. For a moment he wanted to shout. Instead he looked at the ground and said quietly, "She wasn't just a dog to me. I need some time." Mateo scratched his neck. "Oh. Okay." Later Tomas found his older sister at the fence, and she put her arm around him without saying anything.

qa.q: What did Mateo tell Tomas to do?
qa.a: He told him to just get a new one.

qa.q: What was Tomas feeling when Mateo said it was only a dog?
qa.a: Hurt; his throat tightened, he felt like shouting, and to him Luna was family.

qa.q: What did Tomas do that helped him after the hurtful comment?
qa.a: He calmly told Mateo he needed time and then turned to his sister, who understood without trying to fix it.

qa.q: How might Mateo see the moment?
qa.a: He probably thought a new dog would solve the sadness, and his scratching his neck and quiet "Oh. Okay." suggest he realised he had said something that stung.

grounding: A child grieving a dog is stung by a friend's dismissive remark, tells him gently he needs time, and turns to someone who understands.
